key_facts: A **painless lump, sinus or scar over neck nodes**, or a chronic plaque, in someone from a high-incidence area or with TB contact.
*M. tuberculosis* reaching skin from a deeper focus, by inoculation or blood spread; **tuberculids** are immune reactions.
Refer to the **TB service** for biopsy, culture and treatment (NICE NG33); contact screening; HIV test.
Pulmonary or disseminated TB, **HIV**, and **rifampicin interactions**.

sections.title: Overview
blocks: Skin infection by *Mycobacterium tuberculosis* complex (rarely *M. bovis* / BCG). Uncommon in the UK but seen in people from high-incidence countries, the immunosuppressed (HIV, anti-TNF, steroids), homeless people and those with prior TB contact. **Scrofuloderma** is the commonest form in many series: TB of an underlying structure (usually **cervical lymph node**, also bone/joint/epididymis) breaks through to the skin. Case 1 is a classic scrofuloderma with active pulmonary TB.

blocks: **Mechanism in Case 1:** pulmonary TB → lymphatic spread to cervical nodes → caseating necrosis → cold abscess → direct (contiguous) extension through overlying dermis → nodules, ulcers, sinuses.

fig.caption: Scrofuloderma: a caseating lymph node in the neck tracks up through a sinus to an undermined, dusky ulcer on the skin; healing leaves puckered cord-like scars.
fig.alt: Neck cross-section with caseating node and sinus to the skin

ul: **Scrofuloderma:** firm, **painless**, initially skin-coloured then **dusky red/blue** subcutaneous nodules over the **neck** (submandibular, supraclavicular, anterior triangle), axilla, groin, chest wall; nodes **matted, non-tender** ("cold"). Nodules soften, discharge cheesy/watery material, form **undermined ulcers and sinus tracts**, healing slowly with **cord-like, puckered scars** and skin bridges.
Systemic: chronic cough, weight loss, night sweats, fever (Case 1).
**Lupus vulgaris:** slowly enlarging red-brown plaque on head/neck; diascopy shows **"apple-jelly" nodules**; scarring, tissue destruction; risk of SCC in long-standing lesions.
**TB verrucosa cutis:** warty plaque on hands, knees, buttocks.

**Tuberculids:** crops of necrotic papules on extensor limbs (papulonecrotic); tiny lichenoid follicular papules on trunk in children (lichen scrofulosorum); tender violaceous nodules on posterior calves of women that may ulcerate (erythema induratum).

ul: Skin/node **biopsy**: caseating granulomas; **Ziehl–Neelsen** stain for AFB; **mycobacterial culture** (gold standard, weeks; gives drug sensitivity); **TB PCR / GeneXpert** (rapid, rifampicin resistance).
Node FNA/excision; sputum smear/culture (AFB+ in Case 1); **chest X-ray**.
**Mantoux / IGRA** support infection but do not separate latent from active disease (may be false-negative in HIV/miliary TB).
**HIV test** for every patient with TB (NICE NG33); also hepatitis B/C, LFTs, renal function, visual acuity (ethambutol) baselines.

ul: **Not managed in primary care** — refer **urgently** to the local **TB service** (respiratory/ID) and dermatology; suspected pulmonary TB with cough needs same-day advice and infection-control (mask, avoid waiting rooms).

Standard regimen (NICE NG33, specialist-initiated): **2 months RHZE** (rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol) then **4 months RH** (longer for CNS/bone, drug resistance). Directly observed therapy where adherence risk. Pyridoxine with isoniazid in at-risk patients.
TB is a **notifiable disease** (the diagnosing clinician notifies UKHSA); **contact tracing** via the TB service.

ladder.t: **Urgent** TB service referral; TB is notifiable; contact tracing via the TB team.
**2 months RHZE** then **4 months RH** (NICE NG33); longer for CNS / bone or resistance. DOT if adherence risk; pyridoxine with isoniazid if at risk.

**Interaction check** for rifampicin: contraception, warfarin / DOACs, antiretrovirals, antiepileptics, methadone, steroids, azoles. Counsel: orange urine and tears (stains soft lenses); report jaundice, dark urine, vomiting; ethambutol → report colour-vision change.

blocks.title: Prescribing limits and pitfalls
list: **Contraception**: Rifampicin defeats combined hormonal contraception: non-hormonal / IUD (FSRH).
**Don’t**: Repeatedly treat a chronic neck sinus with flucloxacillin.

refer.t: Cough, haemoptysis, weight loss, night sweats: urgent chest assessment with infection control.
Chronic painless neck lump or sinus, especially from a high-incidence country: **TB until proven otherwise**.

sections.title: Red flags and when to refer

ul: Cough, weight loss, night sweats or haemoptysis: urgent chest assessment.
Rifampicin is a strong enzyme inducer: review every interacting drug (contraceptives, anticoagulants, antiretrovirals).

pearls: **Interaction checker is essential:** rifampicin is a potent enzyme inducer — reduces efficacy of combined hormonal contraception (advise non-hormonal/IUD/medroxyprogesterone with adjustment per FSRH), warfarin/DOACs, antiretrovirals, antiepileptics, methadone, steroids, azoles. Orange urine/tears (stains soft contact lenses).
Hepatotoxicity (RHZ): counsel to report jaundice, dark urine, vomiting; avoid alcohol; LFT monitoring per specialist.
Ethambutol: report any visual change (colour vision) immediately.
A chronic painless neck lump/sinus, especially with cough, weight loss, or origin from a high-incidence country, is **TB until proven otherwise** — do not repeatedly treat with flucloxacillin.
Skin lesions heal with scarring; tuberculids clear only with anti-TB treatment of the hidden focus.

quiz.q: Commonest form of cutaneous TB in many series?

quiz.a: 2 months rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol, then 4 months rifampicin + isoniazid.
Enzyme induction makes combined hormonal contraception unreliable: use non-hormonal / IUD.
